title: Canada federal CBCA guide pack
description: Federal business corporation guide tracks for CBCA annual maintenance, corporate records, securities registers, and ISC records. Current registered rules are reviewed snapshots; historical application requires a separately verified effective period. Privacy scope is assessed from operations and activities on the Privacy page.

sections.label: ss. 263, 212(1)(a)(iii), 212(2)
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 263, 212(1)(a)(iii), 212(2)

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 1975-12-15 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: A corporation sends an annual return in the period fixed by the Director. Statutory default can lead to notice-based dissolution; the Act requires notice and an opportunity to cure.
content.tooltip: A corporation sends an annual return in the period fixed by the Director. Statutory default can lead to notice-based dissolution; the Act requires notice and an opportunity to cure.
content.caveat: An unfiled return stays outstanding. Dissolution is not automatic at the filing deadline; the statutory one-year default ground and registrar practice are distinct.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 263, 212(1)(a)(iii), 212(2)

sections.label: ss. 20, 22, 50
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 20, 22, 50

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 1975-12-15 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: Maintain articles/bylaws/amendments and unanimous shareholder agreements, shareholder proceedings, statutory director notices, securities register, accounting records and board/committee proceedings. Electronic records must be intelligibly reproducible and protected. Accounting records are retained six years after the financial year to which they relate.
content.tooltip: Maintain articles/bylaws/amendments and unanimous shareholder agreements, shareholder proceedings, statutory director notices, securities register, accounting records and board/committee proceedings. Electronic records must be intelligibly reproducible and protected. Accounting records are retained six years after the financial year to which they relate.
content.caveat: Canadian accessibility, foreign-location conditions and other statutory retention periods still apply. Six years is not a blanket destruction period for constitutional records, minutes or registers.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 20, 22, 50

sections.label: ss. 114(2)–(4), 139
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 114(2)–(4), 139

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 1975-12-15 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: Unless bylaws provide otherwise, shareholder quorum consists of holders of a majority of shares entitled to vote, present personally or by proxy. Subject to articles/bylaws, board quorum is a majority of the prescribed board number/minimum, with resident-Canadian participation requirements.
content.tooltip: Unless bylaws provide otherwise, shareholder quorum consists of holders of a majority of shares entitled to vote, present personally or by proxy. Subject to articles/bylaws, board quorum is a majority of the prescribed board number/minimum, with resident-Canadian participation requirements.
content.caveat: Class votes, sole shareholders and adjournment rules must be evaluated independently. Voting share count is not simply a headcount of people.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 114(2)–(4), 139

sections.label: ss. 2(1), 6(3), 117, 142
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 2(1), 6(3), 117, 142

provenance.changeNote: Commencement 1975-12-15 restored from the previously verified guide (verified commencement). currentAsOf records only the review of the current wording; amendments after commencement must be checked against the point-in-time text for older meetings.

content.summary: An ordinary meeting resolution uses a majority of votes cast; a special meeting resolution normally needs at least two-thirds. Written shareholder resolutions require all shareholders entitled to vote on that resolution. Written board/committee resolutions require every director entitled to vote.
content.tooltip: An ordinary meeting resolution uses a majority of votes cast; a special meeting resolution normally needs at least two-thirds. Written shareholder resolutions require all shareholders entitled to vote on that resolution. Written board/committee resolutions require every director entitled to vote.
content.caveat: Increased articles/unanimous-shareholder-agreement thresholds and transaction/class rights may apply. Special and annual written resolutions are subject to the statutory director/auditor statement exceptions.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 2(1), 6(3), 117, 142

sections.label: ss. 133, 142
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 133, 142

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 1975-12-15 is the earliest date the governing Act could apply (Canada Business Corporations Act came into force 1975-12-15); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: The first annual meeting is due within 18 months after existence begins. Subsequent meetings must be within 15 months of the preceding meeting and six months of the preceding financial year-end. A valid unanimous written resolution disposing of all required annual business can replace the meeting.
content.tooltip: The first annual meeting is due within 18 months after existence begins. Subsequent meetings must be within 15 months of the preceding meeting and six months of the preceding financial year-end. A valid unanimous written resolution disposing of all required annual business can replace the meeting.
content.caveat: Court extension and the director/auditor written-statement exceptions must be checked. A planned meeting or incomplete ordinary resolution is not annual-business completion.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 133, 142

content.summary: An annual return is due within 60 days after the anniversary of incorporation, amalgamation or continuance, beginning the following year. It cannot be filed before the anniversary. Inactive corporations still file; federal tax returns are separate.

content.summary: Shareholder-meeting notice follows the prescribed range. A non-distributing corporation’s articles or bylaws may specify a shorter minimum. Individual waivers and required special-business/electronic-meeting content are separate rules.
content.tooltip: Shareholder-meeting notice follows the prescribed range. A non-distributing corporation’s articles or bylaws may specify a shorter minimum. Individual waivers and required special-business/electronic-meeting content are separate rules.
content.caveat: A distributing corporation cannot use the private-company shorter-notice exception. No universal ten-day floor appears in s. 135(1.1).

sections.label: ss. 2.1, 21.1
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 2.1, 21.1

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2019-06-13 is the earliest date the governing provisions could apply (the CBCA ISC register provisions commenced 2019-06-13); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: In-scope corporations keep an ISC register, identify controllers through voting/value, direct/indirect and joint-control tests, review it at least once each financial year and record new information within 15 days after awareness. It includes identity, citizenship, tax residence, control and diligence information.
content.tooltip: In-scope corporations keep an ISC register, identify controllers through voting/value, direct/indirect and joint-control tests, review it at least once each financial year and record new information within 15 days after awareness. It includes identity, citizenship, tax residence, control and diligence information.
content.caveat: Public/prescribed exclusions and detailed control tests need entity facts. Former-individual personal information is disposed of in the year after the sixth anniversary of cessation, subject to longer legal retention.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 2.1, 21.1

sections.label: ss. 21.21, 21.303–21.31
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 21.21, 21.303–21.31

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 2024-01-22 is the earliest date the governing provisions could apply (research records the federal ISC filing regime from 2024-01-22); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: ISC information must be sent annually, after specified organizational events and within 15 days of recording changes. The Director makes prescribed selected particulars public; access to the full register is a separate enforcement regime.
content.tooltip: ISC information must be sent annually, after specified organizational events and within 15 days of recording changes. The Director makes prescribed selected particulars public; access to the full register is a separate enforcement regime.
content.caveat: The 15-day internal-update clock runs from awareness; the change-filing clock runs from entry. Old shareholder/creditor full-register access under former s. 21.3 is repealed. Underage and safety-related publication exceptions apply.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 21.21, 21.303–21.31

content.summary: The registry’s filing service implements the January 22, 2024 filing regime: at incorporation, within 30 days of amalgamation/continuance, with the annual return, and within 15 days after a change is entered. An exempt corporation supplies the applicable exclusion confirmation.
content.tooltip: The registry’s filing service implements the January 22, 2024 filing regime: at incorporation, within 30 days of amalgamation/continuance, with the annual return, and within 15 days after a change is entered. An exempt corporation supplies the applicable exclusion confirmation.
content.caveat: These are registry filing instructions under the Act’s Director-fixed requirements. Preserve an actual submission receipt and the relevant reporting cycle.

sections.label: ss. 20(4), 21
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 20(4), 21

provenance.changeNote: Commencement of this wording is not verified. notBefore 1975-12-15 is the earliest date the governing Act could apply (Canada Business Corporations Act came into force 1975-12-15); guidance for earlier review dates carries a commencement caveat.

content.summary: Shareholders, creditors and specified representatives can inspect the shareholder-level records free of charge; directors inspect the broader board/accounting records. Distributing corporations have additional public access. Statutory shareholder-list requests involve an affidavit, permitted purposes, a reasonable fee and the ten-day delivery rule.
content.tooltip: Shareholders, creditors and specified representatives can inspect the shareholder-level records free of charge; directors inspect the broader board/accounting records. Distributing corporations have additional public access. Statutory shareholder-list requests involve an affidavit, permitted purposes, a reasonable fee and the ten-day delivery rule.
content.caveat: Shareholder status does not confer blanket inspection of directors’ minutes, accounting books or the full ISC register.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, ss. 20(4), 21

sections.label: s. 103
sections.citation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, s. 103

content.summary: Subject to articles/bylaws/unanimous shareholder agreement, directors can make, amend or repeal bylaws effective immediately and submit them to the next shareholder meeting for ordinary confirmation, amendment or rejection. Failure to submit or shareholder rejection ends their effect.
content.tooltip: Subject to articles/bylaws/unanimous shareholder agreement, directors can make, amend or repeal bylaws effective immediately and submit them to the next shareholder meeting for ordinary confirmation, amendment or rejection. Failure to submit or shareholder rejection ends their effect.
content.caveat: Ordinary CBCA bylaws are kept internally, not routinely filed with Corporations Canada. Do not import federal not-for-profit bylaw filing requirements.
content.displayCitation: Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, s. 103

content.summary: Fundamental articles amendments normally require a special resolution, any separate class/series approval and filing of articles of amendment; they take effect under the resulting certificate.
content.tooltip: Fundamental articles amendments normally require a special resolution, any separate class/series approval and filing of articles of amendment; they take effect under the resulting certificate.
content.caveat: A director/address notice or ordinary bylaw resolution does not substitute for an articles amendment. Transaction-specific rules and dissent rights can change the workflow.
